listening.title: Campus Canteen Allergy Information Desk
listening.focus: understanding allergy information and service details
listening.script:
STAFF: Good morning, Allergy Information Desk, David speaking. How can I help you?
MAYA: Hello, I'm Maya, a new Environmental Science student. I have a serious nut allergy, so I wanted to ask about the food before I order lunch.
STAFF: Of course, Maya, I'm happy to help. We keep a detailed allergy list for every dish. Is there a particular meal you want?
MAYA: Yes, I was looking at today's menu. I wanted the chicken pasta, but I'm not sure if it's safe for me.
STAFF: Let me check the list for you. Today's chicken pasta contains milk and wheat, but it does not have any nuts or peanuts as ingredients. However, please check with the kitchen about preparation and cross-contact controls before ordering.
MAYA: That's a relief. What about the vegetable soup? My friend said it is very good.
STAFF: According to our ingredient list, the vegetable soup does not contain any of the main allergens as ingredients — no milk, no wheat, no nuts, and no eggs. However, please also check with the kitchen about preparation and cross-contact controls before ordering.
MAYA: Wonderful. Do I need to book my lunch in advance because of my allergy?
STAFF: Not for the regular menu. You can just order at the main counter. However, if you need a special meal made without milk or wheat, you should inform the kitchen at least one hour before you want to eat.
MAYA: I understand. And how can I check the allergy information myself next time?
STAFF: That's easy. We place small green allergy cards next to every dish at the counter, and you can also scan the QR code on each table to see the full ingredient list on your phone.
MAYA: That's very helpful. One last question — what time do you stop serving lunch?
STAFF: Lunch service finishes at 3 p.m. — sorry, I mean 3:30 p.m. on weekdays. At the weekend, we close earlier, at 2 p.m.
MAYA: Thank you. Is there any charge for the allergy cards?
STAFF: No, there is no charge at all. You can take a card with you for free.
MAYA: Great, thanks for your help.
STAFF: You're welcome, Maya. Please come back anytime if you have more questions.

reading.title: The Campus Garden Tool-Loan Service
reading.focus: how the service works and its benefits
reading.passage:
The Campus Garden Tool-Loan Service was started two years ago by the university's Environment Office. It is located in a small building behind the Science Centre and is open to all registered students, not only those studying gardening or agriculture. The main aim is to help students grow plants without buying expensive equipment. Staff at the office say the idea came from student requests for cheaper ways to garden in small flats and dormitories.

To use the service, students must first register once at the office with their student ID card. After registration, they can book tools online through the university website. Most tools can be borrowed for seven days, and students can extend the loan for another seven days if no one else has booked the same item. If tools are returned late, there is a small fee of two dollars per day. This system keeps the tools available for everyone.

The service offers many useful hand tools such as spades, forks, rakes, and watering cans. Larger items like wheelbarrows are also available, but the service does not lend large machines such as petrol lawnmowers because they need special training and are difficult to store. Students can see photos and availability of each tool on the booking page before they choose. Every tool is checked by staff when it is returned, and broken tools are repaired quickly so they are ready for the next user.

Before borrowing for the first time, each student must attend a short 20-minute safety session. In this session, staff explain how to use and clean the tools correctly. Students must return all tools clean and on time. The author claims that this simple rule is the most important reason the service works well. For example, last term one group returned muddy tools late, and other students could not use them for two days. This example shows what happens when the rule is not followed, but the claim itself is about the importance of the rule in general.

Since the service began, more students have started gardening on campus and at home. A recent survey of 200 users showed that 80% saved money by borrowing instead of buying, and many said they learned new practical skills. The garden behind the library, which was empty before, is now full of student plots. Overall, the tool-loan service has created a stronger sense of community and made gardening easier for beginners. The Environment Office plans to add more tools next year if funding is approved.

exercises.title: The Campus Garden Tool-Loan Service
exercises.focus: how the service works and its benefits
exercises.passage:
The Campus Garden Tool-Loan Service was started two years ago by the university's Environment Office. It is located in a small building behind the Science Centre and is open to all registered students, not only those studying gardening or agriculture. The main aim is to help students grow plants without buying expensive equipment. Staff at the office say the idea came from student requests for cheaper ways to garden in small flats and dormitories.

To use the service, students must first register once at the office with their student ID card. After registration, they can book tools online through the university website. Most tools can be borrowed for seven days, and students can extend the loan for another seven days if no one else has booked the same item. If tools are returned late, there is a small fee of two dollars per day. This system keeps the tools available for everyone.

The service offers many useful hand tools such as spades, forks, rakes, and watering cans. Larger items like wheelbarrows are also available, but the service does not lend large machines such as petrol lawnmowers because they need special training and are difficult to store. Students can see photos and availability of each tool on the booking page before they choose. Every tool is checked by staff when it is returned, and broken tools are repaired quickly so they are ready for the next user.

Before borrowing for the first time, each student must attend a short 20-minute safety session. In this session, staff explain how to use and clean the tools correctly. Students must return all tools clean and on time. The author claims that this simple rule is the most important reason the service works well. For example, last term one group returned muddy tools late, and other students could not use them for two days. This example shows what happens when the rule is not followed, but the claim itself is about the importance of the rule in general.

Since the service began, more students have started gardening on campus and at home. A recent survey of 200 users showed that 80% saved money by borrowing instead of buying, and many said they learned new practical skills. The garden behind the library, which was empty before, is now full of student plots. Overall, the tool-loan service has created a stronger sense of community and made gardening easier for beginners. The Environment Office plans to add more tools next year if funding is approved.
exercises.prompt: Who is allowed to use the tool-loan service?
exercises.explanation: The passage says the service is open to all registered students, not only gardening students. Option B fails because it limits access incorrectly.

writingPrompts.focus: Summarising a table with trends and comparisons
writingPrompts.prompt:
The table below shows the number of students who attended the campus welcome picnic in 2022, 2023 and 2024, by year group.

Year group | 2022 | 2023 | 2024
First-year students | 85 | 110 | 130
Second-year students | 60 | 65 | 70
Third-year students | 40 | 45 | 50
Total | 185 | 220 | 250

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.

The bar chart below shows the number of times students borrowed sports kits from the campus sports centre from January to May 2024.

Month | Number of borrowings
January | 32
February | 48
March | 54
April | 42
May | 68

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.

writingPrompts.task: Task 2 · Welcome Events for New Students
writingPrompts.focus: Discussing two views and giving a clear opinion with examples
writingPrompts.prompt:
Some people think universities should organise a welcome picnic for new students at the start of each year. Others think it is not necessary and students can meet each other in other ways.

Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.

writingPrompts.task: Task 2 · Borrowing or Buying Sports Equipment
writingPrompts.focus: Explaining reasons and evaluating advantages and disadvantages
writingPrompts.prompt:
Many universities allow students to borrow sports kits for free instead of buying their own. Some students prefer to borrow, while others prefer to buy.

Why do students borrow sports kits? Do the advantages of borrowing outweigh the disadvantages?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.

writingPrompts.task: Task 2 · Joining a Beginner Cooking Class
writingPrompts.focus: Giving a clear position with simple reasons and direct evidence
writingPrompts.prompt:
Some people believe that all university students should join a beginner cooking class to learn basic cooking skills. Others think students are too busy with their studies for this.

Do you agree or disagree? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.

speakingPrompts.prompt:
Let's talk about food and cooking.
Do you like cooking at home or eating outside?
How often do you cook?
Who taught you to cook?
What kind of food do you like to eat with friends?

speakingPrompts.task: Part 1 · Campus Life and Free Time
speakingPrompts.focus: Talking about familiar campus activities and free time
speakingPrompts.prompt:
Let's talk about your campus and free time.
What do you do in your free time on campus?
Do you enjoy outdoor events like picnics?
How often do you do sports or other activities with other students?

speakingPrompts.task: Part 2 · Cue card · A Campus Welcome Picnic
speakingPrompts.focus: Describing a past campus event with details, actions and feelings
speakingPrompts.prompt:
Describe a welcome picnic or outdoor event you went to on your campus.
You should say:
• when and where the event was
• who you went there with
• what food and activities there were
• and explain why you liked or did not like this event.

You will have one minute to prepare and you should speak for one to two minutes.

speakingPrompts.task: Part 3 · Community Events and Practical Skills
speakingPrompts.focus: Evaluating reasons and value of campus events and practical classes
speakingPrompts.prompt:
Let's discuss community events and learning new skills.
Why do universities organise welcome events for new students?
Are large campus events a good way to make new friends? Why or why not?
Do you think practical classes like beginner cooking are as important as academic classes? Why?

speakingPrompts.task: Part 3 · Borrowing and Sharing at University
speakingPrompts.focus: Discussing reasons for borrowing and evaluating university support
speakingPrompts.prompt:
Let's talk about borrowing and sharing things at university.
Why do some students prefer to borrow sports equipment instead of buying it?
What are the advantages and disadvantages of sharing university facilities?
Should universities provide more free services for students? Why or why not?
